analysis.one_liner: Strips product makers of the legal defense that liability warnings given to a doctor or other intermediary shield them from consumer lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors, was never considered by the House Judiciary Committee, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under long-standing 'learned intermediary' case law, a company can escape liability for an injured consumer if it gave complete safety information to a licensed professional — like a doctor or pharmacist — who then dealt with the consumer; drug and device makers invoke this defense most often. This bill would abolish that defense in every U.S. court, allowing injured consumers to sue manufacturers directly even when warnings went through an intermediary [S2][S3]. It never received a hearing or a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Injured consumers who were hurt by a product after a licensed intermediary — a doctor, pharmacist, or similar professional — received the manufacturer's warnings. Today, makers can often defeat those lawsuits entirely by showing they warned the intermediary; this bill would let those cases proceed to a jury [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers injured by products, especially drugs

how_it_helps.text: It removes a defense that currently ends many product-liability lawsuits before they reach a jury, so injured consumers could sue manufacturers directly even when warnings were delivered through a licensed intermediary.

analysis.who_pays: Product manufacturers — especially pharmaceutical and medical device makers — would face broader liability exposure, and some of those costs could pass to consumers through prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: By applying to any product where a licensed intermediary — including a doctor or pharmacist — stands between the maker and the consumer, the bill would sweep in prescription drugs and medical devices, potentially raising liability costs and drug prices and drawing well-documented objections from those industries.

The bill was drafted as a one-page federal rule with no threshold or carve-outs, so even a manufacturer that gave complete, accurate warnings to the prescribing professional could face liability to end consumers — a cost supporters of the bill would have to acknowledge.
It received no cosponsors and no committee action in the two months before the Congress ended, so it was never examined, debated, or refined in any public forum.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a one-sentence rule change that would remove a barrier to lawsuits over defective products, including prescription drugs and devices, but its blunt wording — no exception for properly prescribed pharmaceuticals, no threshold like evidence of a warning defect — would raise liability costs broadly and invite arguments that it replaced carefully balanced state tort law with a federal mandate [S2][S3]. With zero cosponsors and no committee action, no hearing record exists to test whether the benefits would outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in mid-November 2010 with no cosponsors, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on November 17, 2010, with no cosponsors [S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, and on December 20, 2010 to its Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy, where it remained [S5].
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, and the bill never received any further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers — especially drug and medical device makers — that rely on the learned intermediary defense to defeat lawsuits are better off because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 17, 2010 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair John Conyers, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 17, 2010 and never held a markup or reported the bill out.

against.name: Subcommittee on Courts and Competition Policy
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 20, 2010 and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no committee action is recorded, so no positions beyond the sponsor's own can be measured.

industries.note: The learned intermediary defense is most often used in prescription-drug and device cases; eliminating it would expose manufacturers to direct suits from patients, even where a doctor received full warnings [S3]. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against injured consumers' ability to sue.

Any manufacturer whose products reach consumers through a licensed professional — pharmacists, equipment dealers, financial or technical advisors — would lose the defense, facing broader liability exposure [S3].
Plaintiffs' bar groups favor removing defenses that block product-liability suits; the bill would expand the viable claims consumers could bring [S3].
